content: The proposed intervention was evaluated for its potential applications and the precision of its estimated effects. During a meeting in San Francisco, USA, members of the guideline development group were asked to express their positions on the recommendations, as well as their judgments regarding the benefits and harms of the intervention. They also assessed the strength of the recommendations based on several factors: (i) the desirable and undesirable effects of the intervention, (ii) the certainty of the available evidence, (iii) the values and preferences associated with the intervention in various settings, and (iv) the cost and feasibility of implementing the intervention in different contexts. These aspects were openly discussed during the meeting, and each member documented their primary considerations on individual forms. Following this, private deliberations were held among the guideline development group members. The WHO Secretariat compiled and disclosed a summary of the results to the group. If unanimous consensus was not achieved, additional time was allocated for further deliberations, followed by a second round of online voting. If consensus was still not reached, a two-thirds majority vote was required to approve the recommendations. Divergent opinions were allowed to be recorded in the guideline, and the voting results were retained by WHO for up to five years. WHO staff present at the meeting, as well as the systematic review teams involved in evidence collection and grading, did not participate in the consensus-building process. Two co-chairs with expertise in group management and evidence interpretation were nominated at the start of each consultation and approved by the group. As part of the Cochrane pre-publication editorial process, external peer reviewers, including an editor, two referees, and a statistical adviser, provided comments on the reviews. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions outlines the detailed process for preparing and maintaining systematic reviews on healthcare interventions. The guideline on fortifying wheat flour with vitamins and minerals as a public health strategy was developed with the support of the WHO Secretariat, which facilitated the meeting process but did not vote or have veto power. All experts participating in the WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their involvement. The technical officer and relevant departments reviewed these declarations before finalizing the group composition and issuing invitations. Participants acted in their individual capacities, not as representatives of their institutions, and verbally disclosed any potential conflicts of interest at the start of each meeting. Specific declarations of interest were managed according to WHO guidelines. For example, Dr. Hector Bourges Rodriguez disclosed his role as chair of the Danone Institute in Mexico, a non-profit organization funded by Danone Mexico. Since Danone does not produce products related to wheat flour fortification, he was allowed to fully participate in the deliberations. Similarly, Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil disclosed her previous employment with Nutrition International and her role in the Food Fortification Initiative. She was permitted to participate fully but was asked to disclose her affiliations at the start of the meeting. Dr. Maria Elena del Socorro Jefferds, who works for the International Micronutrient Malnutrition Prevention and Control Program, also disclosed her employer’s involvement in supporting wheat flour fortification initiatives. She participated fully in decision-making after disclosing this information. Dr. Lynette Neufeld declared that her employer, the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, supports food fortification programs. Although she was not directly leading any related initiatives, she disclosed her personal and organizational interests in food fortification. Ms. Carol Tom, employed by USAID and a consultant for the East, Central, and Southern African Health Community, declared her affiliations, which were deemed not to present any conflicts of interest. The systematic review teams also declared no conflicts of interest and did not participate in the decision-making process. The WHO Secretariat plans to monitor research developments in wheat fortification, particularly in areas with limited or low-quality evidence. If an update to the guideline is warranted, the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, in collaboration with other WHO departments, will coordinate the update following formal WHO procedures.
